title: How Many Giants Are Mentioned in the Bible?
paragraphs:
How Many Giants Are Mentioned in the Bible?
The Forgotten Truth About the Giants Who Terrified Nations—And Why Their Story Is Really About You
Most people think the story of giants in the Bible is about massive warriors, impossible battles, and ancient mysteries.
It isn't.
Not really.
Because beneath every giant recorded in Scripture is a deeper story.
A story about fear.
A story about weakness.
A story about ordinary people standing before impossible odds.
A story that ultimately points to Jesus Christ.
And maybe that's why the giant narratives continue to grip hearts thousands of years later.
Because somewhere deep inside, every one of us knows what it feels like to stand in front of something bigger than ourselves.
A diagnosis.
A divorce.
An addiction.
A betrayal.
A secret sin.
A shameful past.
A crushing regret.
A future that feels uncertain.
Giants did not disappear after biblical times.
They simply changed form.
The Bible contains several references to giants, and while scholars differ on some details, Scripture consistently presents certain groups and individuals as extraordinary in size and strength.
One of the earliest references appears in Genesis 6:4:
"The Nephilim were on the earth in those days—and also afterward—when the sons of God went to the daughters of humans and had children by them. They were the heroes of old, men of renown."
The Hebrew word used here is נְפִלִים (Nephilim).
The exact meaning remains debated among scholars, but the term is associated with mighty figures whose reputation endured through generations.
Later, when Israel's spies entered Canaan, they reported:
"We seemed like grasshoppers in our own eyes, and we looked the same to them." (Numbers 13:33)
Again they used the term Nephilim.
Notice something important.
The text does not focus on the giants' exact height.
Instead, it reveals the condition of the spies' hearts.
Fear made them feel small.
Fear distorted their perspective.
Fear convinced them that God's promises were weaker than the obstacles before them.
And fear still does the same today.
The Bible also mentions the Rephaim (רְפָאִים, Rephaim), a people known for unusual stature and strength.
King Og of Bashan is one of the most famous examples.
Deuteronomy 3:11 records:
"Only Og king of Bashan was left of the remnant of the Rephaim. His bed was made of iron and was more than nine cubits long and four cubits wide."
Depending on the measurement used, that bed could have exceeded thirteen feet in length.
Scripture does not present this detail to entertain curiosity.
It emphasizes the magnitude of what Israel faced.
God intentionally led His people into situations where victory would be impossible without Him.
Then there is the giant everyone remembers.
Goliath.
His name echoes through history because his story echoes through human experience.
1 Samuel 17 describes him as a Philistine champion whose height measured "six cubits and a span."
The Hebrew text presents him as a terrifying warrior wrapped in armor, carrying weapons so massive that seasoned soldiers trembled at the sight of him.
For forty days he mocked Israel.
For forty days he challenged God's people.
For forty days fear ruled the battlefield.
Then a shepherd boy arrived.
Not a warrior.
Not a king.
Not a military strategist.
A shepherd.
David's confidence was never rooted in his ability.
It was rooted in God's faithfulness.
When David declared:
"You come to me with sword and spear and javelin, but I come to you in the name of the LORD Almighty" (1 Samuel 17:45),
he revealed the true theme of the story.
The giant was never the main character.
God was.
And that remains true today.
The Bible mentions additional giants connected to Goliath's family and the descendants of the Rephaim.
Second Samuel 21 and First Chronicles 20 record several giant warriors defeated by David's mighty men.
Among them were Ishbi-Benob, Saph, Lahmi, and a giant with six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot.
Including Goliath, Scripture identifies numerous giant figures and giant clans, though exact totals depend on how one counts individuals versus groups.
Yet something remarkable emerges from every account.
None of the giants win.
Not permanently.
Not ultimately.
Every giant eventually falls.
Every intimidating enemy eventually collapses.
Every threat eventually encounters the power of God.
This is why the giant narratives have survived for thousands of years.
Because they are not fundamentally stories about height.
They are stories about hope.
They remind us that what appears impossible from a human perspective is never impossible for God.
The greatest giant in your life may not be visible to anyone else.
It may be guilt.
It may be anxiety.
It may be bitterness.
It may be pornography.
It may be depression.
It may be the consequences of a decision you desperately wish you could undo.
It may be the memory of a scandal that still haunts you.
And this is where the Bible's giant stories become deeply personal.
Because the greatest giant humanity ever faced was not Goliath.
It was sin.
The Greek New Testament uses the word ἁμαρτία (hamartia), meaning sin, missing the mark, falling short of God's holy standard.
Every human being stands guilty before a perfectly holy God.
No amount of self-improvement can remove that guilt.
No achievement can erase it.
No reputation can hide it.
No success can redeem it.
That giant is too big for us.
But not for Jesus.
At the cross, Jesus Christ faced the giant none of us could defeat.
He bore our sin.
He carried our shame.
He absorbed the judgment we deserved.
Then three days later He rose again.
The giant fell.
Death fell.
Sin fell.
Condemnation fell.
The empty tomb became heaven's declaration that no giant stands taller than the Son of God.
This is why the Gospel is not merely good advice.
It is good news.
The Bible never says David saved himself.
It never says Israel conquered giants through self-confidence.
And it never says sinners save themselves through religious effort.
Salvation belongs to the Lord.
The Aramaic phrase often spoken by Jesus, אַבָּא (Abba), reveals the intimacy now available to those who trust Him.
Through Christ, enemies become children.
Through Christ, rebels become redeemed.
Through Christ, scandals become testimonies.
Through Christ, broken stories become beautiful stories.
Through Christ, giants become monuments to God's faithfulness.
Maybe that is exactly what you needed to hear today.
Because perhaps you've been staring at a giant for so long that you've forgotten to look at God.
Perhaps you've convinced yourself that your failure is too great.
Your shame is too deep.
Your past is too ugly.
Your addiction is too strong.
Your wounds are too severe.
Your mistakes are too permanent.
But the entire message of Scripture says otherwise.
From Genesis to Revelation, God specializes in rewriting impossible stories.
Abraham was too old.
Moses felt unqualified.
Rahab carried a scandalous reputation.
Peter denied Christ.
Paul persecuted Christians.
Yet grace rewrote every chapter.
And if grace could rewrite theirs, grace can rewrite yours.
That is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
If this article stirred your heart, don't keep it to yourself.
What giant are you trusting God to defeat?
Your testimony may be exactly what another struggling believer needs to read.
Supporting this ministry is one practical way to help spread God's truth to those who desperately need hope.
Because one shared article can reach a wandering prodigal.
One comment can encourage a hurting believer.
One testimony can point a soul toward Jesus.
One act of support can help carry the Gospel farther than you may ever know.
The giant isn't the end of the story.
The God who defeats giants is.
